We’d have to do it all the time, oh what did we do?
Oh what have we done?
And that taught us a lesson. Don’t ever do anything that you wouldn’t be proud to do, you know, over and over.
That’s an excellent rule to remember.
Yeah.
Picture doing this on a gig.
Now you’ve got to do it for the rest of your life.
It’s immediate hell.
There’s some more guidance that I guess came through for you. Did it get released?
Yes.
Yeah it was released, but I think it was — was it on vinyl or — I can’t remember was it a 45?
Throw it out of your mind.
It was quite early.
The song that was Steve Allen’s was called “Oh Banana Split.” That was kind of cute.
[humms]

But I mean we would never dream of singing it now, because I mean that was when we were young and you know you could get away with such cutsie pie stuff. But now I mean, I wouldn’t dream of doing it now. But that’s the way the world goes sometimes. Because he was trying to broaden our audience, and we said well okay, maybe this time we’ll try it. But we’d been told stuff a lot of times, even Joe Glaser, who was our booker

at one time early on. We had a meeting with him, he says, “I don’t know, you kids, you walk a line, you’re not cabaret and you’re not jazz, you’re kind of walking the line there. Do one or the other.” We said well this is who we are, this is what we do, this is what we like.
These are the songs we like. This the music we love.
And we were doing both because we could work both kinds of clubs. It made it better for us.
Does that controversy still come up for you? Are you cabaret or jazz?
Probably.
Occasionally. Just like April 19, the Manhattan Association of Cabarets and Clubs will be honoring us with a Lifetime Achievement Award, at a special function they’re having. So you know—
And of course we got the 50 year anniversary celebration as part of the jazz festival last year.
The JVC Jazz Festival.

JVC Jazz Festival. And so that’s another thing, that’s a jazz thing, but you know, so be it. I don’t care that much about awards, I just want to do what we want to do, and enjoy it, and we make our living doing it, and it’s fun. If we weren’t getting paid for it we’d still be doing it probably. But that’s a bonus. And we get to travel all over, you know, that’s one of the greatest things that we enjoy about it too, we’ve been to Europe, we’ve been to Australia, we’ve been to Japan, we’ve been to Brazil.
Hawaii.
And we get paid.
And you’re not going in a station wagon with column speakers on the top.
That’s right. We’re enjoying seeing the world.
You guys paid a lot of dues and it makes the good times that much better.
Sure.

You also learn a few things traveling. Don’t drink the water. You know you to go San Francisco, and you change water, and all of a sudden you’re feeling strange. You go down to Los Angeles, you drink that water, oh this is weird, it upsets your whole system.
You’re whole system, yeah.
So the evils of the road.

Well that and even food, you know eating out all the time. If you have to eat in restaurants all the time, it’s not as good as what you probably would have if you were eating at home you know. It’s all right to eat out occasionally but when you have to eat out every day, breakfast, and dinner, you have to be careful about your diet if you want to feel good. We tried to, sometimes you do the best you can do, which sometimes is
limited. So that’s another thing that’s important though when you’re traveling, because otherwise your health — you know if you don’t feel good, you can’t work well and do well.

If you were listening, if you had some time and you just wanted to listen to some stuff that you were influenced by when you were young in Chicago, or Milwaukee was it, what records would you pull out to listen to, to revisit your influences?
Teddy Wilson piano; Earl “Fatha” Hines’ big band; Woody Herman’s Thundering Herd; Sonny Stitt, Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis.

As we go, you go. I started out without even a record player listening to the radio. I’m talking about Jo Stafford and you know there were a few people, just hearing songs, good songs, and the singers were pretty good and I could learn them from the radio. And then also getting into more jazz things because I started working with bands around Milwaukee. You know playing stock arrangements most of the time, but I did get to meet a lot of musicians, and they’d say, “hey have you ever heard Billie Holiday — have you ever heard Peggy Lee — have you ever heard” this one, that one. And then I started listening to other people, and going to shows at the Riverside Theater in Milwaukee and I heard Dinah Washington with Lionel Hampton’s band and I thought that was great, I loved her, and I saw Anita O’Day with Gene Krupa on the stage, and going to hear anything that was like that. And I was definitely drawn to jazz because when I’d hear a saxophone playing on the radio, oh, turn the sound up, what’s that.

I would listen to late night radio, I was supposed to be asleep but I would take a small radio under my covers, one of those little radios, and I would listen to Earl “Fatha” Hines broadcast from the Grand Terrace Ballroom in Chicago. And they would come on the air and you’d hear like [scats] and the brass is like [scats]. And then over all this you hear this voice come in and he says “Fatha Hines, Earl, Fatha Hines.” [scats] And I’d listen and and oh God, that’s so wonderful, that’s what I want to do. And I was studying classical piano at the time. And the next morning I’d get up, go to the piano, and I discovered my piano didn’t have those notes on it.
It would take some time to find them, too. Yeah, that’s great.

I used to go into clubs in Milwaukee at times that I was really too young to be in these clubs. But the club owner would kind of overlook the fact that I was there. And I would sit in with different people. There was a group called Eddie Getz, and he was an alto player that Roy knew in the Army actually, and a very good player, and a good rhythm section, I mean as good as I thought they could be at that time.
He was good.
And they’d let me sit in. I guess they thought I wasn’t too bad or they wouldn’t have asked me to come in. They’d always want me to come up. I’d sing “The Man I Love” and

I don’t know what all, the funny songs you know, can’t remember even the rest. That was before I sang “Happiness is a Thing Called Joe” after I heard Frances Wayne sing it. But you know when people say who were your influences, everything you hear is your influence you know? I mean there were so many singers, how can you nail it down to one or two people? As I went along I loved Ella, I loved Billie Holiday of course, who else, Peggy Lee I mentioned.
And your good buddy Sarah Vaughan.

Oh and Sarah Vaughan was a very big influence on me in the early, when I was first working with Roy. Because she was very hot then. She was just coming into prominence. And Dave Garroway is the one who dubbed her “The Divine One.” And he would talk about her all the time and play her records, and I said yeah, she’s great. I sounded like her for a while because sometimes inadvertently people you like, it rubs off on you you know. You’re not trying to copy them really, but it’s just a period of development you know, that you’re learning as you go.
Yes. It’s a sincere form of flattery too.

Yeah. And then at one point I finally got smart enough to say hey wait a minute, you don’t want to sound like somebody else, you want to have your own sound, so — maybe somebody suggested that to me, I don’t remember. But I did realize that I had to — so I started just singing pure and straight ahead, and not too tricky. And the thing that I believe in is that you should serve the song, rather than have the song serve you. So too much stylistic stuff doesn’t make it for me. I mean Sarah, I liked Sarah the best in her early days, the early records. Because she even got almost too stylistic, but she was so wonderful, you couldn’t help but love her.
That vocalisma.

She had such a marvelous instrument and she had such facility with it, and she always did good music and had good groups, so I mean she’s a-okay, and always was. But I liked her early stuff, the way she sang, you know, simpler.

I just remembered that last night, Marian McPartland took us, we were sitting backstage talking, and she took us back to Jump Town, where met and started playing. She said that she and Jimmy McPartland were playing in Chicago.
At the Brass Rail.
At the Brass Rail, and they would rush out after their final set to hear us at Jump Town, night after night after night. And we never knew it.
We never knew it. Yeah that was funny.
And just last night she related that.
Because I did know that they used to come and hear us when we were playing somewhere downtown too, and that was later, with Ventura.
That was with Charlie Ventura.
But I didn’t know that they had come to the other place.
What’s coming up in the near future for you?
We just got back from Florida, we did a concert down there for the Gold Coast Jazz Society, and we didn’t know what to expect because we haven’t been performing in Florida, and it just happened.
I think we only did one job down there, at a club called Bubba’s.
At any rate, we went down and we rehearsed with Don Payne the bass player who we met in Riverdale.
Our friend’s house we used.
And then a guy who’s been with us recording and on tour, Steve Bagley the drummer. And so it was alumni. We rehearsed them and did the concert and it turned out to be wonderful, it was just perfect.
It was in a beautiful little theater, just the right size.

Gorgeous Steinway piano. It played itself, all I had to do was sit there and look. And we did that and then we hung out in Naples, Florida with some of our friends for about five days vacationing. Came home. Opened up the suitcases, emptied them, put them away, and all of a sudden we get a call from John Schriber, he said, “I know it’s kind of sudden, but could you guys appear on Marian McPartland’s 80th birthday on Saturday?” This was Thursday.
Thursday night.

And we said, yeah, sure, why not? We’re here. Okay. And he says, “oh thank you, you saved our lives, because Joe Williams got sick and he’s not going to be able to make it.” So that was it. And then Jackie said why not, for Marian’s 80th birthday, let’s sing that song of hers that she wrote with Peggy Lee. What’s it called?
“In the Days of Our Love,” which is pretty.
So I went looking through music and then I just had to go back 15 years or whatever, two years ago we did it I think.
Well we did it a couple of years ago, once.
To find it, to see what key or what the melody is or what the lyrics are. And so Friday Jackie’s going back and learning this song, that she’s going to do Saturday, with Marian.

Yeah. And I’m not used to working with other pianists very often, because I don’t get to do it that much. You know I’ve done it a few times but not often. And so we ran through it once in the theater, you know, when we came in for the sound check. And her chords sounded so totally different. And it was an odd piece.
Only in a few places. Oh God, she played some beautiful things.
Oh she played beautiful things, yeah. But it did sound different to me, and I don’t know, it was another key for her too, because she didn’t write it in that key. But she’s amazing.
She’s brilliant.
She is brilliant that way. She can do any key.
Bamm just like that she got it.

I mean she’s just great. So we did it last night, and I was like a little nervous on it, and I kind of clenched up there a couple of times. But I got through it, and after I came back to the release after she played a half a chorus, then I got it better, because I had been through it once and, oh yeah, now I remember what it is. That was through though and being a broadcast, you know, a live broadcast, made me feel pressured about it. I probably wouldn’t have been nervous but I was nervous because of that.
And for me it was a great pleasure working with Grady Tate on drums.
And Christian McBride.

And I really loved Christian’s playing. And he’s such a big, warm guy, like he just gives you hugs and says, “yeah, it was good playing with you again.” And with Grady, after we finished, I’m going to tell you this and you can cut it if you like, I went over to him, we went down to the dressing room and I put my arm around him and says, “Grady, it was just wonderful, because playing with you is really a comfort.” And he says “yeah, like a jock strap.”

We know him pretty well because he does the Jazz Nativity with us every year. We’ve been doing that thing for eight, nine years. And this year he sings the opening song. He’s a wonderful singer, as you know. And then of course we see him every year at that, and so we’re always in the same dressing room. Everybody’s in the one dressing room, and there’s a lot of jokes, and that’s one of the things we enjoy about doing that is because we get to hang out with the musicians every year.
Well I want to thank you so much for making it into the city today because I’ve been looking forward to talking to you, and I want to thank you for your marvelous career.
Oh thank you.
And all the records you’ve recorded.
Great, great.
It’s been a grand life and as I said before, I know we’ve had some angelic guidance. Just certain things have come up that you can’t believe, how come?

Yeah, we’ve been very fortunate. We try to honor the music and do the best we can when we’re working, and we just love doing it. So we feel that we’re just so fortunate and so lucky. You know we’re going to do it as long as we can. Very often people say, “do you guys ever think about retiring?” We say why would we? You know, unless we can’t do it anymore. If we don’t sound good enough, if we don’t think we sound good enough to go
out and do it we’ll stop doing it. But if we can make it and keep making it good enough, we will.
Father John, a priest from Boston, said to us, he said, “you two are running your own ministry.”
That was nice. I’ll buy that dream.
All right. Well I hope you enjoy the rest of your evening.
Thank you. We’re going over to hear another favorite, Blossom Dearie. Yeah she’s great. We’re going to hear her tonight. Thank you very much for inviting us.
Thank you, Monk.
You came well — well people spoke of you before we came here and they said oh you’ll love him, you’ll like him. Yeah, yeah.
That’s nice to hear.
And you are very comfortable to talk to.
Appreciate that.
Enjoyed it.
That’s ’cause I’m talking to people who do what I love, and do it well.
Great, thanks.
And thank you, Tim. All right. And God bless us all.
Nothing can be said after that.
‘Twas the best of times, ‘twas the worst of times. Well this is the best.
